title: Landforms and Earth Processes
seo_title: Landform Worksheets: Uplift, Erosion, Deposition and Time Scales (High School Earth Science)
standard_text: Develop a model to illustrate how Earth's internal and surface processes operate at different spatial and temporal scales to form continental and ocean-floor features.
meta_desc: Free high school Earth and space science worksheets on landforms (NGSS HS-ESS2-1): internal and surface processes, agents of erosion, uplift and erosion rates and time scales. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Internal heat raises land; the Sun and gravity drive erosion and deposition.
body_html:
How to think about it

Internal processes build land up; surface processes wear it down.

  • Internal (heat from inside): plate motion, volcanoes, uplift, ridges, trenches, rifts.
  • Surface (Sun and gravity): weathering, erosion and deposition by water, ice, wind and waves.
  • Processes act over seconds (landslides) to hundreds of millions of years (ocean basins). Net change = uplift − erosion.
Example

Uplift 5 mm/yr for 1,000,000 years?

5,000,000 mm

Answer: 5 km

Example

Uplift 3 mm/yr, erosion 1 mm/yr, 100,000 yr?

2 mm/yr × 100,000

Answer: 200 m higher

Common mistakes

  • Thinking mountains stay the same height forever.
  • Thinking erosion builds landforms only.
  • Thinking big landforms form in a few years.

faq.q: What is the difference between internal and surface processes?
faq.a: Internal processes, driven by Earth's heat, build land through plate motion, volcanoes and uplift. Surface processes, driven by the Sun and gravity, wear land down by weathering, erosion and deposition.
Some changes take seconds (landslides) and others take millions of years (mountain ranges and ocean basins).

faq.q: Why do old mountains look rounded?
faq.a: Erosion has worn them down for a long time, and uplift has slowed or stopped.
